newsitem.title: INDIA: Tata group says hopes to rescue India airport deal.
newsitem.headline: Tata group says hopes to rescue India airport deal.

text.p: India's Tata group on Tuesday held out hope of keeping alive a $335-million airport project in southern India even as one of its Singapore partners was getting cold feet over the government's new terms for the deal.
A Tata group official said the group was waiting for the Civil Aviation Ministry to finalise the terms for building the airport in Bangalore city.
"We believe the government's concerns can be addressed within the build-own-operate framework," Eric Vaz, projects manager, told Reuters.
"We have discussed various points of view and we await a response from the ministry," he said.

The government had initially offered the project under conditions that would allow the consortium -- comprising Tata, U.S. firm Raytheon and six Singapore companies -- to build, own and operate (BOO) the airport.
But Indian Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim later insisted the project go ahead under a build, own and transfer (BOT) scheme.
One source in the Singapore consortium said on Monday that the firm planned to withdraw from the project because it did not agree with the new terms.
The Singapore consortium comprises L&M Group Investment SI, RSP Architects, Arcasia Land (formerly Technology Parks), Singapore Technologies, Sembawang Industrial and Parameswara Holdings.

Vaz said: "Only one partner in the consortium, Parameswara Holdings, has expressed certain concerns about BOT. We'll have to wait and see what the terms are. The terms of the project have not yet been finalised."
Vaz said he did not expect the government to reach a decision before next week.

Ibrahim on Tuesday told India's upper house of parliament that the state-run Airports Authority of India was prepared to take over the project if the consortium was unwilling to accept BOT terms, the Press Trust of India said.

"Nowhere in the world is an airport built on BOO pattern," the news agency quoted Ibrahim as saying. He said foreign investment in developing airports was welcome, but ownership must remain with the government.

Ibrahim earlier this year blocked a planned joint venture between Singapore Airlines and the Tata group to set up a domestic airline in order to protect domestic operators. A Tata Industries official said in March it had not given up hope that the deal will eventually go through.
The project at Bangalore, one of India's largest cities, is the first effort to build private airport facilities since India launched an economic liberalisation programme in 1991.
The Tata group holds a 26-percent-stake in the project, Raytheon 24.5 percent and the government of Karnataka state, of which Bangalore is the capital, holds 25 percent.
